fields.definition: The audible change in loudness (and slight change in timbre) that occurs as a bowed-string player reverses bow direction. Because a note's loudness follows bow speed, the bow decelerating to a stop and reversing at each up-bow/down-bow change causes a momentary dip in level, while down-bow and up-bow strokes also carry inherent dynamic tendencies (a down-bow near the frog naturally sounds stronger).
fields.plain_english: A bow only moves one way at a time. When a violin or cello player flips the bow's direction, the sound dips for a moment and its tone can shift a little. It is like the tiny pause you hear when someone saws a board back and forth.
fields.purpose_function: It is an inherent artifact of how a bow drives a string: since volume tracks bow speed, the speed passing through zero at each reversal creates a natural articulation point that players either use musically or smooth over for seamless legato.
fields.practical_application: Engineers recording strings listen for these dips as uneven seams in sustained lines and address them with mic placement, comping, or gentle gain riding rather than heavy compression, which would pump the room tone.
common_mistakes: Assuming up-bow and down-bow are dynamically identical, so a natural bow-change dip gets mistaken for a bad take or player error
Reaching for heavy compression to hide bow-change dips, which pumps the room and dulls articulation instead of smoothing the line
Ignoring bow direction when editing or comping, so splice points land on a bow-change dip and create awkward level jumps
scenario_contexts: Tracking a solo violin legato line where audible dips at each bow change need transparent gain rather than aggressive compression
A cello section sounding uneven because down-bows land louder than up-bows on a repeated figure
Editing a string overdub and choosing splice points that avoid a bow-change level dip

sources: Adler, The Study of Orchestration (W. W. Norton)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (Springer)
J. Woodhouse, Euphonics: the science and technology of musical instruments (euphonics.org, University of Cambridge)

fields.definition: A harsh, noisy, poorly pitched quality in bowed-string tone produced when bow force, bow speed, and distance from the bridge fall outside the range that sustains clean Helmholtz (slip-stick) string motion. It typically results from excessive bow force for the chosen bow speed and bow-to-bridge distance, which turns the note into a raucous 'crunch' rather than a clear pitch; too little force gives a thin, whistling 'surface sound' instead.
fields.plain_english: The scratchy, crunchy sound a violin or cello makes when the bow is used wrong. Press too hard or drag it badly and you get noise instead of a clear, smooth note.
fields.purpose_function: Recognizing it matters because it marks the boundary of playable tone described by Schelleng's bow-force limits, so its presence signals that technique, rosin, or bow position, not the microphone, is the cause.
fields.practical_application: On a session an engineer hearing scratchiness first checks player technique, rosin, and bow-bridge position before suspecting the signal chain, and may move a mic slightly off-axis or further back to reduce captured bow noise.
common_mistakes: Blaming a scratchy string recording on the mic or preamp when it is bow force or position producing surface noise
Over-rosining the bow, which increases grip and can worsen scratch and dust artifacts
Close-miking on-axis directly over the bridge, which exaggerates captured bow-contact scratch
scenario_contexts: A student violinist's take sounds harsh because bow force is too high for how close the bow is to the bridge
Setting mic distance and angle on a fiddle session to tame captured bow scratch
Diagnosing whether harshness on a string stem is a technique problem or a signal-chain fault

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (Springer)
J. Woodhouse, Euphonics: the science and technology of musical instruments (euphonics.org, University of Cambridge)
C. E. Gough, 'Violin Acoustics,' Acoustics Today (Acoustical Society of America), 2016

fields.definition: The point along the string where the bow contacts it, expressed as its distance from the bridge as a fraction of the vibrating string length. It ranges from near the bridge (sul ponticello, brighter, thinner, harmonically rich) to over the fingerboard (sul tasto, softer, rounder, fewer high harmonics), and it sets the usable minimum and maximum bow force for a clear tone.
fields.plain_english: Where between the bridge and the fingerboard the player draws the bow. Closer to the bridge is brighter and edgier; over the fingerboard is softer and mellower.
fields.purpose_function: It is a primary tone control for bowed strings: bow position governs harmonic content and how much bow force the string tolerates before the note breaks up or thins, so players use it for both timbre and dynamics.
fields.practical_application: Engineers exploit it by asking a player to move sul tasto for a soft pad or sul ponticello for an edgy effect, and by aiming or placing mics aware that near-bridge playing radiates more high-frequency energy.
common_mistakes: Confusing bowing position (bridge-to-fingerboard contact point) with the fingering position of the left hand on the string
Assuming closer to the bridge simply means louder, when it means brighter and demands more, better-controlled force
Fixing mic placement without accounting for how far from the bridge the part is actually played
scenario_contexts: Directing a violinist sul tasto for a soft, airy sustained texture
Capturing an aggressive sul ponticello effect for a film cue
Choosing mic distance on strings where the player varies bow position across a phrase

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (Springer)
J. Woodhouse, Euphonics: the science and technology of musical instruments (euphonics.org, University of Cambridge)
Adler, The Study of Orchestration (W. W. Norton)

fields.definition: The region of a stringed instrument immediately surrounding the bridge, where string vibration is transferred into the top plate or soundboard and radiated as sound. In recording it is a common microphone and pickup placement zone, and in playing, bowing or picking closer to the bridge yields a brighter, more articulate, harmonically richer tone.
fields.plain_english: The part of a guitar or violin right around the bridge, the small mount the strings rest on. It is a favorite spot to point a mic, and playing near it sounds brighter and snappier.
fields.purpose_function: It matters because the bridge is where string energy enters the body, making the surrounding area acoustically live, a strong and articulate source for miking and the zone where playing distance most changes brightness and attack.
fields.practical_application: Engineers place or aim a mic, or clip a contact pickup, near the bridge to get a direct, attack-rich sound on acoustic guitar or upright bass, balancing it against a warmer, fuller position further from the bridge.
common_mistakes: Miking directly over the bridge or soundhole on acoustic guitar and getting a boomy, boxy tone instead of moving toward the 12th fret for balance
Assuming the bridge area sounds the same as over the soundhole, when the two positions capture very different tonal balances
Confusing the bridge with the nut or saddle when describing a placement
scenario_contexts: Positioning a small-diaphragm condenser near the bridge of an acoustic guitar for attack and clarity
Clipping a contact pickup at the bridge area of an upright bass for live reinforcement
Comparing bridge-area versus 12th-fret mic positions to dial in an acoustic guitar's brightness

sources: C. E. Gough, 'Violin Acoustics,' Acoustics Today (Acoustical Society of America), 2016
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (Focal Press)

fields.definition: The process by which a stringed instrument's bridge couples string vibration into the body and thereby into radiated sound. Driven by the string, the bridge rocks and bounces on the top plate to excite the body's radiating modes, and its own resonances create a broad 'bridge hill' response peak around 2-3 kHz that shapes brightness and presence.
fields.plain_english: The bridge is the small part the strings rest on. It passes the strings' shaking into the body, which then moves the air so you can hear it. The bridge also rings a little on its own, adding brightness around 2 to 3 kHz.
fields.purpose_function: It exists because strings alone move too little air to be heard; the bridge acts as a mechanical coupler and filter that transfers and colors string energy on its way to the radiating body, strongly influencing tone and projection.
fields.practical_application: Knowing the bridge hill sits near 2-3 kHz helps an engineer understand where a violin's presence and edge live, guiding mic choice and gentle EQ, and explains why adding a bridge mute rolls off the highs by many decibels.
common_mistakes: Treating the bridge as a passive mount rather than an active, resonant coupler that colors the tone
Assuming a heavier bridge or a mute only lowers volume, when it also strongly attenuates high frequencies
Expecting EQ alone to fully restore the presence lost when a mute damps bridge radiation
scenario_contexts: Explaining why a muted violin loses air and edge on a recording
Choosing a mic and a gentle EQ move that flatters the 2-3 kHz bridge-hill presence region
Comparing two violins whose brightness differs largely because of bridge mass and setup

sources: C. E. Gough, 'Violin Acoustics,' Acoustics Today (Acoustical Society of America), 2016
J. Woodhouse, Euphonics: the science and technology of musical instruments (euphonics.org, University of Cambridge)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (Springer)

fields.definition: A brass-instrument mute (used on trumpet, cornet, and trombone) consisting of a cylindrical container packed with sound-absorbing material such as cotton or felt that clips onto or fits over the bell. It absorbs high frequencies to give a soft, dark, veiled tone without significantly altering pitch.
fields.plain_english: A padded cup that clips over the open end of a trumpet or trombone. It makes the sound soft, warm, and far-away, like hanging a blanket in front of the horn.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to darken and soften a brass instrument's timbre for mellow, subdued passages, filtering out bright high harmonics while the player still articulates normally.
fields.practical_application: In tracking or live sound a bucket-muted horn is much softer and duller, so the engineer moves the mic closer or adds gain and eases off the high-frequency EQ used for an open horn.
common_mistakes: Confusing the bucket mute (absorbent cylinder over the bell) with a cup mute (hard cup), which sound different
Miking a bucket-muted horn as if it were open and getting a thin, distant, low-level signal
Assuming any mute drastically changes tuning, when the bucket mute mainly changes timbre and level
scenario_contexts: A big-band trumpet section using bucket mutes for a soft ballad backing
Recording a muted trombone where the engineer must add gain and back off treble EQ
Selecting among straight, cup, and bucket mutes to match a soft, dark tone brief

sources: Adler, The Study of Orchestration (W. W. Norton)
Piston, Orchestration (W. W. Norton)

fields.definition: A guitar signal-chain device containing a unity-gain buffer amplifier, a stage with very high input impedance and low output impedance that copies the signal's voltage without changing its level. It isolates a high-impedance magnetic pickup from cable capacitance and following loads, preserving high-frequency content over long cables and true-bypass pedal chains.
fields.plain_english: A small box that strengthens a guitar's signal without making it louder. It lowers the signal's impedance so the sound can run through long cables and many pedals without losing its bright, sparkly highs.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to solve tone loss: a passive pickup has high impedance, and long cables and stacked bypassed pedals form a filter that dulls the highs, so a buffer's low output impedance drives that load cleanly and keeps the signal bright and strong.
fields.practical_application: Players place a buffer near the start (and sometimes end) of a large true-bypass pedalboard, or use a pedal with a good built-in buffer, to stop the rig sounding dull, and engineers reference it when a guitar loses clarity over long runs.
common_mistakes: Thinking a buffer boosts volume, when it is unity gain and changes impedance, not level
Assuming true-bypass is always best, when a long all-true-bypass chain can dull tone that a buffer would preserve
Placing a buffer before a fuzz or vintage wah that needs to see the guitar's high impedance, changing how those effects respond
scenario_contexts: A large pedalboard sounding dull, fixed by adding a buffer to drive the cable load
Long cable runs on a stage darkening a guitar tone
Deciding buffer placement so a fuzz pedal still interacts properly with the pickups

sources: Ballou (ed.), Handbook for Sound Engineers (Focal Press)
Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (Cambridge University Press)

fields.definition: A clamp fitted across all the strings of a guitar or similar fretted instrument at a chosen fret, shortening the vibrating string length to raise the pitch of every string by the same interval. It lets a player use familiar open-string chord shapes in a higher key.
fields.plain_english: A clamp that presses down all the strings at one fret. This makes the whole guitar sound higher. Now easy chord shapes work in a new key. Think of it as a spare finger laid across the neck.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to transpose an instrument up in fixed semitone steps without new fingerings, keeping the ringing open-string sound in keys that would otherwise require barre chords.
fields.practical_application: In the studio a capo lets a guitarist match a singer's key while keeping bright open voicings, and engineers note capo position because it shifts the instrument's register and resonances, affecting mic placement and doubling.
common_mistakes: Clamping too hard or off-center behind the fret, which pulls strings sharp and causes buzzing; place it just behind the fret with minimal pressure
Assuming a capo needs no tuning check, when fitting it can pull strings slightly sharp and require retuning
Forgetting the capo changes the sounding key, causing transposition errors when reading chord charts
scenario_contexts: A session guitarist capoing up to keep open-chord voicings in the vocalist's key
Doubling a part with one guitar open and another capoed for a shimmering layered sound
Rechecking tuning right after fitting a capo before a take

sources: Denyer, The Guitar Handbook (Alfred A. Knopf)
The New Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments (Oxford University Press)

fields.definition: In an accordion, a tone chamber (Italian cassotto, literally 'little house') built into the treble side through which one or more reed banks, usually the lower 16-foot and/or 8-foot sets, sound. The chamber acts as a passive acoustic filter that attenuates high overtones, giving a warmer, rounder, more mellow timbre.
fields.plain_english: A small sound box inside nicer accordions. Some of the reeds play through it. This gives a warmer, softer, less nasal tone, a bit like singing into a cupped hand.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to refine tone: by enclosing certain reeds it softens their bright, reedy overtones so those registers sound rounder and more vocal, a feature prized on higher-end instruments.
fields.practical_application: When miking an accordion an engineer captures a notably darker sound from the cassotto reed banks than from the brighter non-cassotto reeds, and may mic the treble side to balance the two.
common_mistakes: Assuming cassotto changes pitch or tuning, when it only shapes timbre and tone color
Expecting every reed bank to sound through the chamber, when typically only the 16-foot and 8-foot banks are in cassotto
Miking an accordion at one fixed spot and missing the tonal difference between cassotto and non-cassotto registers
scenario_contexts: Recording a jazz or musette accordionist and choosing cassotto registers for a warm solo tone
Balancing mics across the treble side to blend cassotto and non-cassotto reeds
Explaining why a premium accordion sounds mellower than an entry-level one

sources: The Cambridge Companion to the Accordion (Cambridge University Press)
The New Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments (Oxford University Press)
